title: Comparative Performance of Kenyan and Imported Artemia in Early Larval Rearing of Clarias gariepinus
content:
ABSTRACT

Successful larval rearing of fish depends largely on live feed availability, during the critical first-feeding stage. In Kenya, hatcheries commonly use phytoplankton or imported Artemia cysts as starter feeds, although locally produced Artemia is available. Hatchery operators' reports on low larval survival when using imported Artemia prompted this study to compare growth performance and survival of Clarias gariepinus larvae fed Kenyan-produced and imported Artemia. A 21-day feeding trial was conducted using 12 glass aquaria (60 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm), each containing 30 L of water. A total of 5400 larvae (mean initial weight 1.83 mg; mean initial length 6.09 mm) were stocked at 15 larvae L−1. Three dietary treatments, each replicated four times were tested: Kenyan-produced Artemia (KMFRI strain), Great Salt Lake Artemia (GSL) and Shell-Free Artemia (SFA). Larvae were fed exclusively on Artemia from Day 3 to Day 8 post-hatch, co-fed with Artemia and dry starter feed from Day 9 to Day 11 and thereafter fed exclusively on dry starter feed until Day 21. No significant differences (p > 0.05) were observed in mean total length among treatments throughout the trial. Body weight differed significantly (p < 0.05) on Day 7 with SFA-fed larvae showing superior growth. Survival was also significantly higher (p < 0.05 in SFA-fed larvae compared to encapsulated treatments. Although the KMFRI strain contained lower crude protein content, it supported larval growth comparable to imported GSL. These findings suggest that seven days of live feeding are sufficient for efficient larval rearing of C. gariepinus. There is also an indication that the KMFRI strain has a potential as a locally available live feed to be used in African catfish hatcheries. However, studies on nutritional quality and comprehensive economic evaluation should be undertaken before its commercial adoption.
